title: A rare case of H3K27-altered diffuse midline glioma with multiple osseous and spinal metastases at the time of diagnosis
case_prompt: A 24-year-old man presented with a 10-day history of thoracic back pain radiating to his right shoulder, associated with increased sweating over his right upper body and face and decreased sensation in his right chest. On examination, he had right thoracic pain, gait disturbance, right-sided hypoesthesia, hemi-hyperhidrosis, a positive right Babinski sign, increased reflexes in the right arm and leg, and ataxia consistent with posterior-column involvement. Cranial nerves were intact, there were no motor deficits or meningism, and bladder function was preserved. MRI of the spine showed a large intramedullary lesion extending from C5 to T7 with multiple contrast-enhancing lesions at the craniocervical junction and throughout the spinal cord, as well as heterogeneous vertebral signals suggestive of osseous involvement. Brain MRI demonstrated multiple periventricular contrast-enhancing lesions. CT of the thorax and abdomen revealed diffuse osseous metastases of the entire spine and sternum but no lesions in other organs. Lumbar-puncture CSF analysis revealed atypical cells concerning for leptomeningeal spread, although the cell count was too low for immunohistochemical studies.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. CNS lymphoma was considered given the patient’s age, clinical symptoms, and MRI findings but was excluded when immunohistochemistry indicated a glial origin — “The combination of the patient’s age, clinical symptoms, and MR imaging first led to the suspected diagnosis of a CNS lymphoma, a germ cell tumor, or a glioma leading to interdisciplinary discussions and, of course, a delay in appropriate treatment.” “Immunohistochemical analyses confirmed a glial origin (detection of MAP 2, Olig2, and GFAP positivity).”  
2. A germ cell tumor was considered for the same clinical and imaging features but was ruled out by glial marker positivity on immunohistochemistry — “The combination of the patient’s age, clinical symptoms, and MR imaging first led to the suspected diagnosis of a CNS lymphoma, a germ cell tumor, or a glioma …” “Immunohistochemical analyses confirmed a glial origin (detection of MAP 2, Olig2, and GFAP positivity).”  
3. Metastatic systemic malignancy was considered because of diffuse intraosseous lesions but was excluded when staging CT showed “No other tumorous organ lesions were found within the abdominal or chest cavity.”  
4. Diffuse midline glioma was diagnosed when biopsy revealed the H3K27M mutation with loss of H3K27 trimethylation — “The mutation of histone 3 (H3K27M, Fig. 5 C) with loss of trimethylated lysine (H3K27-m3, Fig. 5 D) in that position was detected.”
